concept: Fake-IP, split-DNS and utun tunnel route changes as false TCP-down/DNS-up diagnoses
summary: Source-anchored research for Fake-IP, split-DNS and utun tunnel route changes as false TCP-down/DNS-up diagnoses. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: A successful name lookup followed by a TCP timeout can result from route selection even when DNS returned an answer. Apple says the system routing table can supersede NetworkExtension included and excluded VPN routes. A macOS two-utun troubleshooting report describes a hostname resolving to 10.99.99.99 while a broad 10/8 route sent TCP and ICMP over the wrong utun; route -n get exposed the selected interface. (medium confidence)

The 2023 USENIX Security study demonstrates that VPN route exceptions can be manipulated to send traffic outside the protected tunnel. Its threat model concerns routing-based traffic leaks; it does not establish that routine macOS fake-IP or split-DNS TCP failures share that cause or measure how often they occur. (low confidence)

A macOS dual-VPN report describes an internal hostname resolving to 10.99.99.99 while TCP and ICMP timed out: an aggregate 10.0.0.0/8 route through utun0 captured traffic intended for a second tunnel on utun15. The report recommends checking `route -n get <IP>` to see which route handles the resolved address before treating the symptom as DNS failure. (medium confidence)

For a VPN configured with includeAllNetworks set to true, Apple documents that the transition from disconnected to connecting leaves existing TCP connections open but drops their subsequent packets; when that VPN leaves connected state, the system drops network traffic. A TCP timeout during this tunnel transition can therefore occur without a DNS lookup failure. (high confidence)

A Versa support article reports the converse case after VPN disconnect: hostname resolution can fail while direct IP connectivity remains available when the VPN and underlay use the same DNS server IP and the system resolver remains pinned to a defunct utun path. DNS failures after a tunnel transition are therefore possible and should be checked directly. (low confidence)

Mihomo fake-IP mode can return synthetic addresses such as the documented 198.18.0.1/16 range. Its TUN documentation says macOS defaults to dns-mode disabled when unset and cannot automatically hijack DNS requests sent to the local network. A Clash Verge report shows the resulting resolver-path split: the system resolver returned router DNS results while Mihomo returned fake IPs; a direct request failed while a request forced to the fake IP succeeded. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-22)

A TCP-down/DNS-up symptom does not identify one root cause. Mihomo advises selecting the outbound interface explicitly when multiple interfaces are active. In an August 11, 2026 follow-up on the Clash Verge report, another commenter said enabling Mihomo sniffing restored connectivity without changing the TUN stack, strict-route setting, or TCP port 53 hijack. Check resolver results, the route and outbound interface, and the client's request logs before assigning the failure to DNS or a utun route. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-11)

Apple configures packet-tunnel DNS resolver settings separately from IP included and excluded routes. `NEDNSSettings.matchDomains` selects DNS settings by hostname, while `NEIPv4Settings.includedRoutes` selects IPv4 destination traffic for the TUN interface. A live utun or route therefore does not establish which resolver answered a name, and a successful DNS answer does not establish which interface carries traffic to its IP. (high confidence)

Apple's NEDNSSettings.matchDomains selects which DNS queries use the tunnel resolver; nonmatching names use the system default resolver. Apple also documents that a VPN which becomes the network's default route uses its configured DNS servers as the default resolver and ignores matchDomains. A successful lookup alone therefore does not show which resolver produced the answer. (high confidence)

A Clash Verge Rev report updated on 2026-08-11 showed TUN routes through utun1024 while `scutil --dns` still selected the router on en0. System resolution returned real IPs, local Mihomo DNS returned 198.18.x.x Fake-IP addresses, and a forced request to a Fake-IP address received HTTP 302 while the ordinary request timed out. This case shows that TUN route presence alone did not prove the system resolver was using the intended Fake-IP path. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-11)

Implementation inference from the split-DNS guide and the two-utun route report: inspect scutil --dns for resolver selection, then use route -n get <returned-IP> and test TCP to that same destination. A direct dig query to a named DNS server checks that server, while an application request tests the resolver and route path that the application actually uses. (medium confidence)
